beats.say: A German author added up the Middle Ages, and found three centuries missing.
beats.headline: IS IT REALLY 1729?
beats.short_title: Did 300 Years of History Never Happen? 🕳️ Verdict on the Viral One #1
beats.bonus: The Phantom Time theory (Heribert Illig, 1991) says AD 614 to 911 were invented, so it's really about 1729. Busted: Chinese astronomers logged Halley's Comet in 837 right where orbital math puts it, eclipse records and tree-ring chronologies line up, and the 1582 calendar fix only reset the calendar to AD 325, not to Julius Caesar's time.

beats.caption: Viral claim: 300 years of the Middle Ages never happened (Phantom Time). Meatball's verdict.
sources: Wikipedia, Phantom time conspiracy theory: proposed by Heribert Illig in 1991; claims Otto III and Pope Sylvester II invented AD 614-911 (297 years); refuted by ancient eclipse records (Pliny, AD 59), Tang-dynasty Chinese observations and Halley's Comet, dendrochronology and archaeology; the Gregorian reform (1582) restored the calendar to AD 325 (Council of Nicaea), not 45 BC, which explains Illig's 'missing' days — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantom_time_conspiracy_theory (checked 2026-10-26)
Ethik und Sozialwissenschaften 8 (1997), critical discussion of Illig's thesis by historians
Halley's Comet 837 apparition recorded in Chinese and European annals — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet (apparitions table)

beats.say: Real or fake years? Guess before I tell you.
Subscribe. A new viral verdict every Wednesday.
See, in 1991, Heribert Illig said Emperor Otto the Third faked the calendar.
His idea: put Otto on the throne in the year one thousand, by inventing six fourteen to nine eleven.
Wait, it gets worse. That deletes Charlemagne, and he's in every textbook.
If he's fake, I'm three centuries younger. I'm not ready to be a baby.
Old churches from back then? Illig says they're misdated.
Thousands of documents? Forged by monks, he says.
But here's the thing. Nobody can forge the sky.

beats.headline: THE MAN WITH TWO FACES?
beats.short_title: The Man With Two Faces Never Existed 😳 Verdict on the Viral One #2
beats.bonus: Edward Mordrake (Mordake), the English heir with a whispering second face, first appeared on 8 December 1895 in the Boston Sunday Post, in an article by fiction writer Charles Lotin Hildreth that cited a 'Royal Scientific Society' that didn't exist then. A medical encyclopedia copied it in 1896 from that 'lay source'. No record of the man has ever been found.

beats.caption: Viral claim: Edward Mordrake, the man with two faces. Meatball traced it to an 1895 newspaper.
sources: Wikipedia, Edward Mordake: apocryphal; first known appearance 8 December 1895, Boston Sunday Post, 'The Wonders of Modern Science' by fiction writer Charles Lotin Hildreth, citing reports of a 'Royal Scientific Society'; copied into Gould & Pyle, Anomalies and Curiosities of Medicine (1896), credited to a lay source — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Mordake (checked 2026-10-26)
USA Today fact check (2021): the only known 'Royal Scientific Society' was founded in 1970 in Jordan; Royal Society of London records have nothing on the cases
Alex Boese, Museum of Hoaxes, 'The Legend of Edward Mordake' (traces the story to Hildreth's 1895 article)

beats.say: The same article had a woman with a fish tail and a man with four eyes.
And the author, Charles Lotin Hildreth, was a fiction writer.
Verdict: no record he ever lived. Just a newspaper story.
A hundred and thirty years later, it's still going viral.
